benvenuto.sottotitolo: What to see in the sky, when, where and with which instrument. Here's how it works:

ss.didascalia: The Solar System seen from above, from the North Pole side. The positions of the planets are the real ones for the day shown, calculated with Astronomy Engine. The distances, however, are not to scale: the orbits are drawn at equal steps, otherwise Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars would all be crammed into a tiny dot around the Sun. The sizes of the planets are made up too. Tap a planet to open its guide.
ss.foto.alt: The Sun and the eight planets in a row, at their real sizes
ss.foto.didascalia: The real sizes: on the right a slice of the Sun, then from right to left Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The distances between them, however, are not to scale.
ss.nota.distanze: "From the Sun" is the average distance; "From us" is the distance on the day shown, and it changes a lot because the Earth moves too.
ss.leggere.1: All the planets go round the Sun in the same direction and almost on the same plane, like marbles on a big plate. That's why we always find them in the same band of sky, the zodiac. The planets close to the Sun race along, the distant ones are very slow: try the "1 month" and "1 year" buttons to watch them move.
ss.leggere.2: When a planet is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun, it can be seen all night and is at its best (this is called opposition). When it's behind the Sun, on the other hand, its light is lost in the glare of daytime.
ss.distanze.vere: If the Sun were a football in St Peter's Square in Rome, the Earth would be a peppercorn 24 metres away, Jupiter a hazelnut 120 metres away and Neptune a pea more than 700 metres away. In between, almost nothing but empty space.

strumenti.sottotitolo: Telescopes, observatories, satellites and probes that have helped us discover the sky: from Galileo's spyglass to the James Webb Space Telescope.
strumenti.luce.1: Our eyes see only a small part of light. Stars and galaxies also send out light we can't see: radio waves (cold gas, pulsars), microwaves (the light of the Big Bang), infrared (heat, stars being born in dust), ultraviolet and X-rays (extremely hot gas, around black holes).
strumenti.luce.2: The atmosphere blocks much of this light: that's why radio telescopes stay on the ground, while X-ray telescopes and many infrared ones go into space. Large telescopes on the ground are built high up, in deserts, where the air is dry, still and far from city lights.
strumenti.fonti: Sources: NASA, ESA, ESO, INAF, Museo Galileo and the websites of the individual observatories.

aiuto.lingua: The app is available in 15 languages. To change language, tap 🌐 at the top or the button below.
aiuto.stasera.1: It tells you what time the Sun sets, when the sky is truly dark and what the Moon is like. Below you'll find what you can see: the direction (north, south, east, west) and the height in "fists". A closed fist at arm's length covers about 10 degrees of sky: "2 fists" means two fists above the horizon.
aiuto.stasera.2: With the buttons at the top, choose Now, Tonight (when it gets dark) or any day and time you like.
aiuto.luogo: Tap 📍 at the top and use your phone's location or choose the nearest town. The app remembers it.
aiuto.guida: On the page of a constellation, star, planet, the Moon, a galaxy, a cluster or a nebula, tap 🧭 Guide me in the sky with my phone, then Start the guide (on iPhone and iPad, confirm the permission). Hold the phone in front of you with the screen facing you and follow the messages: "turn right", "raise the phone"... When you get there, the phone vibrates and the figure of the constellation appears over the sky, or the map with a circle around the object: spread your fingers or tap ＋ to zoom in. With 📷 you see the sky through the camera. Keep metal objects and magnets away: they upset the compass. If the device has no compass, you'll find the direction and height in words below.
aiuto.schede.1: The Moon, planets, stars, all 88 constellations, galaxies, clusters and nebulae. For each one you'll find what it is, when and where to look, with which instrument, the origin of its name and its history. Tap an object in the "Tonight" list to open its guide.
aiuto.schede.2: The "Constellations" and "Galaxies" guides tell you whether they can be seen from the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America etc.) or from the northern hemisphere (all of Europe, North America and Central America etc.): choose "Constellations" or "Galaxies" and then a hemisphere filter. There are also the moons of all the planets, the ones found around exoplanets orbiting other stars, and the ancient legends behind the names in the sky. With the "Search" box you'll find a guide straight away.
aiuto.legenda:
A little key:
The northern (or boreal) hemisphere isn't something limited to a single country: it's the whole half of the Earth lying north of the equator.
The southern (or austral) hemisphere is the whole half of the Earth lying south of the Equator
aiuto.strumenti: Forty-two guides to telescopes, observatories, satellites and probes: from Galileo's spyglass to the James Webb Space Telescope. For each one you'll find what it is, where it is, what it discovered, the origin of its name and a few curiosities.
aiuto.manuale: The course manual, in thirteen chapters, opens with the password given to people taking the course. It is written in Italian only.
aiuto.notte: The 🔴 Night button turns everything red: that way the screen doesn't dazzle you and your eyes stay adjusted to the dark.
aiuto.installa: On Android, choose "Install app" or "Add to Home screen" from the browser menu. On iPhone, in Safari tap the Share button and then "Add to Home Screen". Once installed, the app works even without a connection.
crediti.intro: The real photos of the objects aren't ours: they come from public archives that allow them to be used, as long as the author is credited. Tap the name of the website to see the original page.
crediti.mappe: The sky maps are drawn by the app using star data from {d3} (Olaf Frohn, BSD licence). The drawings of planets, galaxies and nebulae are illustrations made for the app. The mythical figures over the constellations are drawings by Johan Meuris for {stellarium} ({licenza} licence). The positions of the Sun, Moon and planets are calculated with {motore} (Don Cross, MIT licence).
aiuto.scrivi: For questions, problems or suggestions, write to {email}.
aiuto.autore: Cielo di Stasera, by Antonio Chitano.
